glossary.def: The two chief annual magistrates of the Republic, elected by the comitia centuriata, holding full imperium and alternating the fasces monthly. They commanded armies, presided over the Senate and assemblies and gave their names to the year (eponymous dating). Opened to plebeians by the leges Liciniae Sextiae (367 BC); from 342 one consul could be, and from 172 both sometimes were, plebeian. Minimum age 42 under the lex Villia annalis (180) as revised by Sulla. Under the empire consuls became honorific, with suffect pairs every few months; the ordinary consulship survived until 541 (last private holder Anicius Faustus Albinus Basilius).

A consul elected to replace one who died or resigned during the year. From Augustus, regular suffect pairs shortened terms (often two to four months) to multiply consular rank for governorships and commands; the ordinarii of 1 January still named the year.

Magistrate with imperium below the consuls. The urban praetor (from 367 BC) administered justice among citizens; the peregrine praetor (c. 242) cases involving foreigners. Numbers rose to govern provinces (four by 227, six by 197), eight under Sulla, sixteen under Caesar. Each issued an edict setting out the remedies he would grant, the main engine of Roman private law until Hadrian fixed the edictum perpetuum (c. 130).

Two senior magistrates elected (from 443 BC) usually every five years for 18 months to conduct the census, assign citizens to tribes and classes, revise the rolls of Senate and equites (lectio senatus, with the nota censoria for moral failings), let public contracts and build public works, and close the census with the lustrum. Held almost always by ex-consuls; the pinnacle of a career. Lapsed under the empire after Claudius and Vespasian took the office; Domitian became censor perpetuus (85).

Two plebeian aediles (from 494 BC) and two curule aediles (from 367) responsible for the city: streets, temples, markets and weights, the grain supply and public games (Ludi Romani, Plebeii, Megalenses). Lavish games bought popularity for higher office, so the aedileship was costly; Caesar's aedileship of 65 bankrupted him for a time. Not a compulsory step in the cursus.

Lowest regular magistracy, managing finance: the urban quaestors ran the aerarium; others served as paymasters and deputies to consuls and governors. Eight from 267 BC, twenty under Sulla, who made it the qualifying office for automatic Senate membership; forty under Caesar, twenty again under Augustus. A bond of quasi-filial loyalty linked a quaestor to his commander.

Ten plebeian officers (two at first, from 494 BC; ten by 457) elected by the concilium plebis to protect plebeians (ius auxilii). Sacrosanct; could veto (intercessio) any act of a magistrate, election or senatus consultum, and propose plebiscites, binding on all after 287. The Gracchi, Saturninus, Sulpicius and Clodius used it as a popular weapon; Sulla gutted it (81) and Pompey and Crassus restored it (70). Augustus took tribunicia potestas without the office.

Extraordinary single magistrate named by a consul on the Senate's request for a specific task (causa), with supreme imperium for at most six months or the duration of the task, unaccompanied by appeal or tribunician veto in the early period; 24 lictors. Causae included rei gerundae (war), comitiorum habendorum (holding elections) and clavi figendi (driving the sacred nail). Disused after 202 BC; revived without time limit by Sulla (82) and Caesar (perpetual, 44), then abolished by the lex Antonia.

The dictator's deputy, chosen by him and subordinate to him, nominally commanding the cavalry. Famous clashes: Papirius Cursor tried to execute his magister Fabius Rullianus (325 BC); Minucius Rufus was voted equal imperium with Fabius Maximus (217). Mark Antony and Lepidus served Caesar in the role.

A patrician senator appointed for five days when both consulships were vacant, to hold consular elections; successive interreges followed until elections were held (the first interrex never held them). Revived in 82 BC to propose Sulla's dictatorship and used in 52 when riots prevented elections, before Pompey became sole consul.

The senator placed first on the censors' list and therefore first asked his opinion in debate; a position of great prestige (auctoritas) held by the senior patrician ex-censor in the early period. Holders included Scipio Africanus, Aemilius Lepidus, Aemilius Scaurus. Augustus was enrolled princeps senatus in 28 BC, one root of the title princeps.

Head of the college of pontiffs, overseeing state cult, the calendar, sacred law and the Vestals and flamines; residence in the Domus Publica by the Regia. Elected by 17 of the 35 tribes from the 3rd century BC. Caesar was elected in 63 BC; Augustus took it on Lepidus' death (12 BC) and all emperors held it until Gratian dropped the title (c. 379 or 383). Popes later used pontifex.

Boards of three to six (later up to six) military tribunes with consular power elected in place of consuls in 51 years between 444 and 367 BC. Ancient explanations: to admit plebeians without opening the consulship, or to provide more commanders. The number of colleges increased in the warlike years around Veii. Abolished by the Licinio-Sextian laws.

Two boards of ten men with supreme power who replaced the regular magistrates in 451-449 BC to codify the law, producing the Twelve Tables. The second board under Appius Claudius became tyrannical (the Verginia story) and was overthrown by the second secession of the plebs. Other decemviral boards included those for sacred rites and for land assignment.

Six senior officers per legion in the Republic, 24 elected by the people for the first four legions from 311 BC; young nobles began careers here. Under the empire each legion had one senatorial tribunus laticlavius (second in command) and five equestrian angusticlavii.

A promagistrate acting in place of a consul: first in 326 BC (prorogation of Publilius Philo's command at Neapolis), becoming normal for provincial governors. Sulla's system sent consuls and praetors to provinces after their year; Pompey's law of 52 imposed a five-year gap. Under the empire, governors of 'public' provinces (Africa, Asia) bore the title; Augustus held imperium proconsulare over his own provinces.
Promagistrate with praetorian imperium, used for provincial governors and subordinate commanders; legates of the emperor governed imperial provinces as legati Augusti pro praetore.

Extension of a magistrate's imperium after his year in office (prorogatio) or grant of imperium to a private individual (privatus cum imperio, like Scipio in Spain in 210 BC or Pompey in 77). The device that made provincial empire administrable and later concentrated huge commands (Pompey's under the leges Gabinia and Manilia).

An envoy or delegated officer. In the Republic, senators appointed by the Senate as ambassadors or as staff officers to commanders (Caesar's legates in Gaul commanded legions). Under the empire, the legatus Augusti pro praetore governed imperial provinces and the legatus legionis commanded a legion.

Attendants who walked before magistrates carrying the fasces and clearing the way: 12 for a consul, 6 for a praetor (2 within the city), 24 for a dictator. Lictors carried out floggings and executions ordered by magistrates.

Bundle of rods tied with red thongs, with an axe added outside the pomerium, symbolizing a magistrate's power to beat and execute. Lowered (fasces summittere) before the assembled people as a sign of the people's sovereignty; wreathed in laurel after victory.
Folding ivory stool reserved for the 'curule' magistrates (consul, praetor, curule aedile, censor, dictator), an Etruscan-derived symbol of judicial authority, with the toga praetexta.

The ordered sequence of offices in a senatorial career: quaestor, (aedile or tribune), praetor, consul, optionally censor, with minimum ages and two-year intervals fixed by the lex Villia annalis (180 BC) and Sulla (81 BC: quaestor at 30, praetor 39, consul 42). Imperial careers added military tribunates and the vigintivirate before the quaestorship and posts as legate and governor after the praetorship; equestrians had a parallel procuratorial cursus.

Twenty junior magistracies (the board of three moneyers, the three in charge of executions, four for street cleaning in Rome, ten judges of the centumviral court) that young senatorial sons held before the quaestorship under the Principate; earlier 26 (vigintisexviri).

The supreme power of command and jurisdiction held by consuls, praetors, dictators and promagistrates, conferred by a lex curiata. It included command of armies, coercion (coercitio) and capital jurisdiction outside the city, symbolized by the fasces and axe. Limited inside the pomerium by provocatio and tribunician intercession. Imperium could be greater (maius) or equal (aequum) to another's.

The right and duty of magistrates to take the auspices (consult the will of Jupiter through signs such as birds, lightning or the feeding of sacred chickens) before public acts. Patricians originally monopolized the auspices; their claim that only they could take them was a pretext against plebeian consuls. Obnuntiatio (announcing unfavourable signs) could block assemblies, as Bibulus tried against Caesar in 59 BC.

The legal power of any magistrate to act within his sphere (issue edicts, convene bodies, fine), distinct from imperium. Magistrates were classified as having greater or lesser potestas (maior/minor), which determined who could veto whom.

The citizen's right to appeal to the people against a magistrate's capital or corporal punishment inside Rome, traditionally established by a lex Valeria of 509 BC (reaffirmed 449 and 300) and extended by the leges Porciae (early 2nd century) to citizens everywhere. Gaius Gracchus' law of 123 forbade execution without trial, the basis of the debate over the Catilinarians in 63.

The right of a magistrate to block the act of an equal or lesser colleague, and of tribunes of the plebs to veto any act of any magistrate (except a dictator, in the early period). Tiberius Gracchus' deposition of his vetoing colleague Octavius (133 BC) was a constitutional rupture.

The Republican principle that every magistracy (except the dictatorship) was held by at least two equal colleagues, each able to block the other; combined with annuality to prevent a return of kingship.

(1) The 'first triumvirate' of Pompey, Crassus and Caesar (60/59 BC) was a private political alliance, not an office. (2) The triumviri rei publicae constituendae (Antony, Lepidus and Octavian), created by the lex Titia of 27 Nov 43 BC for five years with consular powers, renewed at Tarentum (37) until 33: a legal triple dictatorship that carried out the proscriptions.

In the regal and early Republic a deputy left in charge of Rome when the magistrates were away. Augustus made it a permanent senatorial post for policing Rome, with the urban cohorts; in late antiquity the prefect of Rome (and from 359 of Constantinople, the eparch) governed the city and presided over its senate.

'First citizen': the informal title Augustus preferred, signalling a magistrate-like leadership within restored Republican forms rather than kingship. The resulting system (the Principate, 27 BC to the 3rd century) rested on a bundle of powers (proconsular imperium, tribunician power, control of the army and treasury) voted to each emperor, as in the lex de imperio Vespasiani.

Name voted to Octavian on 16 January 27 BC ('revered', with augural associations), adopted by all subsequent emperors as the title of the senior ruler; from 161 (Marcus and Lucius) there could be two or more Augusti. Women of the dynasty could be Augusta (first Livia, AD 14).

Originally the cognomen of the Julii Caesares, it became part of every emperor's name, and from Hadrian's adoption of Aelius (136) the title of the designated heir. In the Tetrarchy the junior emperors were Caesares under the Augusti.

Victorious general acclaimed by his troops, a title held by Republican commanders until their triumph. Octavian used Imperator as his first name (praenomen imperatoris); emperors counted imperatorial salutations (IMP VII etc.) for victories won under their auspices, and from Augustus only members of the imperial house could be acclaimed (the last private acclamation was Junius Blaesus, AD 22).

The powers of a tribune of the plebs (sacrosanctity, veto, right to propose laws and convene the Senate) held by Augustus without the office from 23 BC and renewed annually; emperors numbered their years by it (TR P). Conferral on a colleague (Agrippa, Tiberius) marked a designated successor.

Proconsular imperium superior to that of other governors, granted to Augustus (from 23 BC) and to delegated princes such as Agrippa, Germanicus (in the East, AD 17) and Corbulo. Gave the emperor command over every army and governor.

Equestrian commander of the Praetorian Guard, created by Augustus (2 BC), usually two in office; became the most powerful official after the emperor (Sejanus, Plautianus) and acquired judicial and administrative duties (jurists Papinian and Ulpian held it). Constantine removed its military role and created regional prefectures (Gaul, Italy, Illyricum, Oriens) that ran taxation, the annona and supply, with appellate jurisdiction: the apex of the late Roman civil hierarchy.

glossary.term: prefect of the grain supply (praefectus annonae)
glossary.def: Equestrian official established by Augustus (c. AD 8) to manage the supply and distribution of grain to Rome from Egypt, Africa and Sicily, including contracts with shippers (navicularii).
Equestrian commander of the vigiles, Augustus' 7,000-strong fire brigade and night police (AD 6), with seven cohorts each covering two of the city's fourteen regions.

Equestrian governor of Egypt with legions under his command, a post closed to senators, who could not even enter Egypt without permission, because of the province's grain and wealth. The first prefect, Cornelius Gallus, fell in 26 BC.

Senatorial governor of an imperial province, appointed by and responsible to the emperor, holding delegated imperium for an indefinite term (usually three years); ex-consuls governed the great military provinces (Syria, Germania, Britain, Pannonia), ex-praetors the one-legion ones.

Senatorial commander of a legion under the Principate, normally an ex-praetor in his thirties. Gallienus excluded senators from such commands (c. 262), replacing them with equestrian praefecti legionis.

Agent managing property for another. Under the empire, equestrian (or freedman) officials managing the emperor's estates, provincial finance (procurator provinciae, who collected taxes in imperial provinces and spied on governors) or governing small provinces (Judaea, Raetia, Noricum, the Alpine and Mauretanian provinces). Pontius Pilate was praefectus, later such governors were styled procurators.

glossary.term: imperial secretariats (ab epistulis, a rationibus, a libellis)
glossary.def: The central bureaux of the Principate: correspondence (ab epistulis, split into Latin and Greek), accounts (a rationibus), petitions (a libellis), legal inquiries (a cognitionibus). Under Claudius run by powerful freedmen (Narcissus, Pallas, Callistus); transferred to equestrians from the Flavians and Hadrian. Evolved into the late Roman scrinia under the magister officiorum.

Informal advisory body of friends (amici), jurists and officials consulted by the emperor on legal and political matters, as in Juvenal's satire of the turbot council. Became the formal sacrum consistorium in late antiquity.

Title of the emperor's wife, mother or sister, first given to Livia by Augustus' will (AD 14). Augustae (Julia Domna, Julia Mamaea, Helena, Pulcheria, Theodora, Martina) could wield great influence; in the East an Augusta could confer legitimacy on a new emperor, as Pulcheria did on Marcian (450) and Ariadne on Anastasius (491).

Diocletian's system of four rulers: two Augusti (Diocletian, Maximian) and two Caesares (Galerius, Constantius) from 1 March 293, each with his own army, court and capital (Nicomedia, Milan, Sirmium/Thessalonica, Trier), bound by adoption, marriage and the divine identities Jovius and Herculius. Planned succession by merit collapsed after the abdications of 305, ending in Constantine's sole rule (324).

Modern term (from dominus, 'lord') for the autocratic late Roman monarchy from Diocletian, contrasted with the Principate: court ceremonial (adoratio, proskynesis), the emperor sacred and remote, separate civil and military hierarchies. Recent scholarship stresses continuity and treats the contrast as overdrawn.

Council of ex-magistrates (c. 300 members in the middle Republic, 600 after Sulla, 900+ under Caesar, 600 again under Augustus) that advised magistrates by senatus consulta. In practice it directed foreign policy, finance, war and provincial assignments. Under the empire it remained a court, a body of governors and the source of legitimacy; in late antiquity there were two senates (Rome and Constantinople) and the senatorial order grew to thousands of clarissimi. The Roman senate is last heard of c. 603.

The meeting place of the Senate: the Curia Hostilia, burned at Clodius' funeral (52 BC), was replaced by Caesar's Curia Julia (completed 29 BC), whose Diocletianic rebuilding survives in the Forum. Also one of the 30 archaic divisions of the citizen body (curiae) underlying the comitia curiata, and in the provinces the town council.

Oldest assembly, organized by the 30 curiae; by the late Republic represented by 30 lictors. Passed the lex curiata conferring imperium on magistrates and witnessed adoptions (Clodius' transfer to the plebs in 59 BC) and wills.

Assembly of the people in 193 centuries arranged by wealth class and age (iuniores, seniores), originally the army in civil form, meeting on the Campus Martius outside the pomerium. Elected consuls, praetors and censors, declared war, and heard capital appeals. The 18 equestrian and 80 first-class centuries held a majority of 98, so voting often stopped before the poor voted; reformed c. 241 to align centuries with the 35 tribes.

Assembly of all citizens voting in 35 tribes, presided over by a consul or praetor; elected quaestors, curule aediles and military tribunes and passed laws. Each tribe had one vote decided by majority within it; the four urban tribes were outnumbered by 31 rural ones, favouring landowners able to come to Rome.

Assembly of plebeians only, voting by tribe, convened by a tribune of the plebs; elected tribunes and plebeian aediles and passed plebiscita, binding on all citizens after the lex Hortensia (287 BC). Most Republican legislation was passed here, including the Gracchan laws.

A public meeting summoned by a magistrate to address the people, without voting; where laws were explained, debated and denounced before the voting assembly. Crucial to late Republican popular politics.

Territorial voting and census unit. Four urban and an increasing number of rural tribes (21 by 495 BC) reached 35 in 241 BC, after which new citizens were added to existing tribes; enrolment of freedmen and the new Italian citizens after 89 BC in particular tribes was fiercely contested.
Voting unit of the comitia centuriata, nominally 100 men, and in the army a company of (in the empire) 80 men under a centurion.

The five census classes of the 'Servian' system, defined by property qualifications in asses (first class 100,000 asses in Livy's account), which determined military equipment and voting weight in the comitia centuriata; below them the capite censi.

Citizens below the lowest property class, registered only by their heads; also called proletarii (contributing only offspring). Exempt from legionary service until the minimum qualification was lowered and Marius openly enrolled them as volunteers (107 BC).
Citizens without property worth registering, counted only as producers of offspring (proles). Effectively the same as the capite censi; manned the fleets in the Punic Wars.

Citizens with property above the minimum census, liable for legionary service and the tributum. The supposed shrinkage of the assidui through war and the spread of large estates was the premise of Tiberius Gracchus' land law.

A decree of the Senate: formally advice to a magistrate, in practice authoritative. Records survive in inscriptions (SC de Bacchanalibus 186 BC; SC de Cn. Pisone patre AD 20). Under the empire senatus consulta acquired the force of law.

The 'final decree' (videant consules ne quid res publica detrimenti capiat) urging magistrates to defend the state by any means, first passed against Gaius Gracchus (121 BC), then against Saturninus (100), Lepidus (77), Catiline (63) and Caesar (Jan 49). Its legality, overriding provocatio, was contested by populares.
Ratification by the patrician senators of decisions of the assemblies; the lex Publilia (339 BC) and the lex Maenia required it to be given in advance, making it a formality.
A resolution of the concilium plebis proposed by a tribune; binding on the whole people after the lex Hortensia (287 BC), and thereafter the main form of legislation.

A statute passed by an assembly on the proposal (rogatio) of a magistrate, named after its proposer's nomen (lex Iulia, lex Sempronia). Laws were posted for three market days (trinundinum) before the vote; voting became secret by the leges tabellariae (139-107 BC).

Declaration by the Senate that a citizen was an enemy of the state, outlawing him: used against Marius and his allies (88 BC), Lepidus (77), Catiline (63), Antony (43), Nero (68) and later emperors and usurpers.

First written Roman law code, drawn up by the decemvirs (451-450 BC) and displayed in the Forum. Fragments quoted by later authors cover procedure (summons, debt bondage with the debtor cut in parts, 'partes secanto'), family (a father selling his son three times loses potestas), property, burial and torts. Cicero says boys learnt it by heart.

Laws of the tribunes Gaius Licinius Stolo and Lucius Sextius (367 BC) that ended consular tribunes, opened the consulship to plebeians (Sextius the first plebeian consul, 366), limited holdings of public land (500 iugera, probably anachronistic) and eased debts.

Law of the dictator Quintus Hortensius (287 BC), passed after the last secession of the plebs, making plebiscites binding on all citizens without patrician ratification; conventionally the end of the Conflict of the Orders.
Law of the tribune Lucius Villius (180 BC) fixing minimum ages for magistracies and a two-year interval between them, regularizing the cursus honorum.

Law of the tribune Aulus Gabinius (67 BC) giving Pompey an extraordinary command against the pirates for three years, with imperium equal to governors' up to 50 miles inland, 500 ships and 24 legates; he cleared the Mediterranean in three months. Followed by the lex Manilia (66) giving him the Mithridatic command.

Bronze tablet (found in Rome, now in the Capitoline Museums) preserving the end of the law or senatus consultum of December 69 conferring powers on Vespasian, with precedents from Augustus, Tiberius and Claudius, including a discretionary clause to do whatever he judged in the public interest.

Edict of Caracalla (212) granting Roman citizenship to virtually all free inhabitants of the empire, except the dediticii (exact meaning disputed). Dio says the motive was to extend the inheritance tax; papyri show a flood of new 'Aurelii'. Made the citizen/non-citizen distinction obsolete, replaced by honestiores and humiliores.
Law applying to Roman citizens, from the Twelve Tables, statutes and juristic interpretation, as opposed to the law of peoples.
The 'law of nations': rules applied to relations involving non-citizens, developed especially by the peregrine praetor; jurists also used it for institutions common to all peoples (sale, slavery).

The annual edict in which each praetor announced the legal remedies (actiones, exceptiones) he would grant; carried over and expanded by successors, it was codified by the jurist Salvius Julianus on Hadrian's orders (c. 130) and then frozen.

Classical civil procedure: the parties appeared before the praetor, who issued a written formula defining the issue, then a private judge (iudex) decided the case. Gradually replaced by cognitio extra ordinem.

Procedure in which an official (emperor, prefect, governor) heard and decided a case himself from start to finish; spread under the Principate and became the only procedure in late antiquity, with appeals up the hierarchy.

Permanent jury court for a particular crime, first for extortion by governors (lex Calpurnia de repetundis, 149 BC), later for treason, murder, electoral bribery (ambitus) and others under Sulla. The composition of the juries (senators or equites) was a central political issue from Gaius Gracchus (122) to the lex Aurelia (70).

Recovery of money illegally taken by Roman officials from provincials; the first standing court (149 BC). Cicero's prosecution of Verres (70 BC) is the classic case; the lex Iulia of 59 tightened the rules.

Crime of diminishing the majesty of the Roman people: originally for incompetent commanders (lex Appuleia, c. 103 BC); under Tiberius extended to words and acts against the emperor, fuelling the trials and informers (delatores) Tacitus describes.
Archaic charge of high treason, tried before the people, as in the trial of Horatius and, revived as a show, of Gaius Rabirius (63 BC).

The father's legal power over his descendants in the male line, including in principle life and death, ownership of all their property and control of marriage, lasting until the father's death unless he emancipated them. Sons could own a peculium; daughters married sine manu stayed in their father's power.

Marriage form in which the wife passed into the power of her husband (or his father), becoming legally like a daughter; created by confarreatio, coemptio or usus. Rare by the late Republic, when marriage without manus left women under their fathers or guardians.

Requirement that adult women not in potestas have a guardian to authorize certain acts; increasingly formal. Augustus' ius trium liberorum freed freeborn women with three children (freedwomen with four).

Privileges granted under Augustus' marriage laws (lex Iulia de maritandis ordinibus, 18 BC; lex Papia Poppaea, AD 9) to parents of three children: faster careers for men, release from guardianship for women, full inheritance rights. Often granted as a favour (Pliny the Younger received it childless).

Freeing of a slave, formally by the vindicta before a magistrate, by enrolment in the census, or by will, which made the freed person a citizen (unlike most ancient societies); informal manumission gave Junian Latin status. Augustus restricted testamentary manumission (lex Fufia Caninia, 2 BC) and set age limits (lex Aelia Sentia, AD 4). Tax of 5% (vicesima libertatis).

A freed slave, a citizen but bound to his former master (patronus) by obligations of respect (obsequium) and services (operae); barred from magistracies and the Senate but prominent in trade and as Augustales. Imperial freedmen (Pallas, Narcissus) ran the Claudian administration.
Property a father or master allowed a son or slave to manage as his own, legally belonging to the head of household; the basis of slave business agency and of slaves buying their freedom.

The legal distinction, crystallizing in the 2nd century and universal after 212, between the 'more honourable' (senators, equites, decurions, veterans) and the 'more humble'. Humiliores faced torture, crucifixion, the beasts and the mines; honestiores exile or beheading.

The emperor's written answer to a petition or official's query, establishing law for the case and as precedent; the bulk of the Codex Justinianus' early material. Petitions answered by subscriptio were posted publicly.

Modern term for official condemnation of a person's memory: erasing names from inscriptions (as Geta's across the empire), destroying statues, annulling acts and forbidding the praenomen. Applied to Sejanus, Caligula (in part), Nero, Domitian, Commodus (later reversed), Geta, Elagabalus, Maximian and others.

Publication of lists of citizens declared outlaws whose killers received rewards and whose property was confiscated: by Sulla (82-81 BC, some 520 named initially and perhaps 4,700 in all) and by the triumvirs (43 BC: 300 senators and 2,000 equites according to Appian, including Cicero).

Inviolability of the tribunes of the plebs, based on the oath of the plebs to kill anyone harming them; violators were sacer. Its violation in the murder of Tiberius Gracchus (133 BC) opened the age of political violence.
Archaic debt bondage in which a debtor pledged his person; abolished by the lex Poetelia Papiria (326 BC), which forbade imprisoning citizens for debt, a key plebeian gain.

Hereditary aristocracy of clans (gentes) claiming descent from the first senators (patres), who monopolized priesthoods and early magistracies. A closed order by c. 450 BC (the Twelve Tables banned intermarriage, repealed by the lex Canuleia of 445). Shrank to some 14 gentes by the late Republic; Caesar and Augustus created new patricians; Constantine's patricius was a personal honour, not a caste.

All citizens who were not patricians, including rich families who formed the plebeian nobility after 367 BC. Organized as a state within the state with its own assembly, tribunes and aediles. Under the empire plebs urbana referred to Rome's citizen population receiving the grain dole.

Modern name for the struggle (494-287 BC) between patricians and plebeians, marked by secessions of the plebs (494, 449, 287), the tribunate, the Twelve Tables, the Licinio-Sextian laws and the lex Hortensia. It produced the patricio-plebeian nobility rather than democracy; ancient accounts are retrojected from late Republican politics.
Collective withdrawal of the plebs from the city, a general strike and military refusal: to the Mons Sacer or Aventine (494 BC), against the decemvirs (449), and to the Janiculum (287).

Originally the cavalry of the 18 centuries with a public horse (equus publicus); by the 2nd century BC a wealthy non-senatorial class with a census of 400,000 sesterces (fixed under Augustus), including publicani, bankers and landowners. Gaius Gracchus gave them the extortion juries. Under the empire, equestrians staffed the procuratorships, prefectures, and the army officer corps; from the 3rd century they displaced senators in governorships and commands.

Families with a consular ancestor (by the most common modern definition, after Gelzer), patrician or plebeian, who dominated the consulship: of some 200 consuls 233-133 BC, only about 15 were 'new men'.
The first man of his family to reach the Senate, and especially the consulship: Cato the Elder, Marius, Cicero.
'The best men': senators defending the Senate's authority and property against popular legislation (Catulus, Cato the Younger, Bibulus). Not a party but a political style and self-description.

Politicians who worked through the people's assemblies and tribunes, often with land, grain or debt measures, against senatorial opposition: the Gracchi, Saturninus, Clodius, Caesar. Usually nobles themselves.

Hereditary relationship of dependence between a patron and clients, involving mutual obligations (fides): legal protection and help from the patron, political support and attendance (morning salutatio) from the client. Extended to whole communities and provinces (the Fabii as patrons of the Allobroges; Pompey in Picenum). Its political weight in elections is debated.

Protector in a client relationship; former master of a freedman; advocate in court; patron of a town or collegium. In late antiquity patrocinium of powerful landlords over villages was repeatedly forbidden by law as a way of escaping taxes.
Morning greeting ceremony at which clients called on their patron's house, ranked by status; size of the crowd measured a great man's standing.

Clan of families sharing a nomen (Cornelia, Iulia), with a praenomen, nomen and cognomen (Publius Cornelius Scipio); agnomina recorded victories (Africanus). Women bore the feminine nomen (Cornelia). The system broke down after 212 when new citizens took the emperor's nomen (Aurelius), and late Romans used single names.
The male head of a familia, the oldest living ascendant, holding patria potestas over his descendants, their spouses in manus, and slaves.
'The custom of the ancestors': the unwritten norms and exempla regarded as authoritative alongside written law, invoked by conservatives against innovation.
An edifying story of an ancestor's conduct (Horatius at the bridge, Mucius Scaevola, Cincinnatus) used in rhetoric and education; Valerius Maximus collected nearly 1,000.
A Roman noble's standing and worth derived from offices, deeds and ancestry, which he was obliged to defend; Caesar justified crossing the Rubicon as protecting his dignitas.
Influence and prestige that commanded deference without legal compulsion. Augustus claimed to have excelled all in auctoritas while holding no more potestas than his colleagues (RG 34).
Good faith and trustworthiness, the bond underlying clientship, contracts and foreign relations (deditio in fidem); deified with a temple on the Capitol.

Large estates, worked by slaves or tenants, often formed from public land; Pliny's 'latifundia perdidere Italiam' (NH 18.35). Archaeology shows medium villas and smallholdings coexisted, so the scale of the 2nd-century BC crisis is debated.

Slaves were property (res) with no legal personality; perhaps 1-1.5 million in Augustan Italy (10-20% of population; some estimate more), from war captives, piracy, birth and exposure. Revolts: Sicily (135-132, 104-100 BC) and Spartacus (73-71). Manumission was frequent. Slavery persisted through late antiquity, though agricultural labour shifted toward coloni.

Originally a farmer or tenant; in late antiquity coloni were tenants tied by law to the land they farmed (from Constantine's law of 332) to secure tax collection, the 'colonate'. Older views of a serf-like class are now nuanced: rules varied by region and class (coloni adscripticii).

Members of the town councils (curiae, ordo decurionum), usually 100 men of property, hereditarily responsible for local government and for collecting imperial taxes, making up shortfalls personally. From the 3rd century burdens drove flight into the army, clergy or imperial service, which laws repeatedly tried to stop.

Senators and their families, with a property qualification of 1 million sesterces under Augustus, the broad purple stripe (latus clavus) and privileges. Late Roman grades: clarissimi, spectabiles and illustres, with only illustres sitting in the Senate by the mid-5th century.

Late Roman honorific grades: vir clarissimus (all senators, by the 4th century thousands), spectabilis (proconsuls, vicars, duces) and illustris (praetorian prefects, magistri militum, palatine ministers); in the 6th century gloriosissimus was added above.

The giving of public benefactions (buildings, games, banquets, oil) by the rich to their cities in return for honour, the motor of urban monumental building in the empire; the term comes from euergetes (benefactor).

Association (professional, religious, burial) with officers and rules; suppressed when politically active (Clodius' collegia, 58 BC) and licensed under Augustus. Late Roman guilds of shippers and bakers were made hereditary.
